newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees freeze-damaged wheat, large corn, soy crops.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees freeze-damaged wheat, large corn, soy crops.

text.p: The Agriculture Department, in its first look at this year's crops, forecast a freeze-damaged winter wheat harvest of 1.56 billion bushels Monday and projected a record soybean crop and the second-largest corn crop.

Assuming normal weather and yields, farmers could harvest 2.60 billion bushels of soybeans and 9.84 billion bushels of corn, the department said. Corn and soybean sowings were the largest since the boom times of the early 1980s.

In a pair of closely watched reports, the government projected an overall wheat crop of 2.26 billion bushels and a cotton crop of 18.5 million bales, both slightly smaller than last year. Wheat plantings were nine percent smaller than last year.

The winter wheat forecast was 13 million bushels lower than expected by traders. The department's projection for all wheat also was lower than expected but corn was higher. Speedy planting was expected to boost corn yields to 131 bushels an acre, three bushels above average.

Large harvests would be needed to meet demand for U.S. crops and to replenish stockpiles. The U.S. supply of soybeans was expected to shrink to 125 million bushels -- lowest in 20 years -- before harvest began and the wheat "carryover" was pegged at a slender 465 million bushels.

Analysts said the most significant figures in the reports were the estimates for the winter wheat harvest and for soybean stocks. Winter wheat, which will be ready for harvest in a few weeks, accounts for the lion's share of U.S. wheat output.
Demand for U.S. soybeans was so strong that consumption was expected to run 118 million bushels higher than last year despite prices likely to average 63 cents a bushel higher.
"The attention seems to be on the soy complex," said analyst Gary Blumenthal of World Perspectives, who called the tentative projections for fall crops "very basic numbers."
Private consultant John Schnittker said large crops this year could easily be swallowed by feedlots and foodmakers with little left over.
"Big crops will simply reduce prices a little more than in the past and we will 'disappear' most of it as we did in the past year," Schnittker said.
Farm-gate prices for this year's corn, soybean and wheat crops were projected to be substantially lower than the levels notched by 1996-crop marketings.

A mid-April freeze hurt a promising winter wheat crop in southwestern Kansas and the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles, lowering output by at least 200 million bushels. Based on May 1 conditions, the three states still would exceed 1996's drought-reduced crop. Subfreezing temperatures in northwest Kansas and southwest Nebraska at the end of last week brought fears of additional damage.

Farmers were speeding through corn and soybean planting at nearly double the usual rate. They intend to plant 68.8 million acres of soybeans, the largest total since 1980, and 81.4 million acres of corn, largest since 1985.
Last year, U.S. farmers reaped 2.28 billion bushels of wheat, including 1.478 billion bushels of winter wheat, 9.29 billion bushels of corn and 2.38 billion bushels of soybeans.
The record for soybean output was 2.517 billion bushels in 1994. The corn record was 10.103 billion in 1994 and the largest cotton crop was 19.66 million bales in 1994.
